question: On a lab test bench, two speeds, in m/s, sum to 3 and multiply to 2; the larger is kept as the speed of a 56 kg slider. A separate thermometer reads 24°C, unrelated to this task. From the slider's kinetic energy, 8 J is subtracted, the total is scaled by a factor of 12, and finally converted into kilojoules. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

On a crane test rig, two acceleration readings, in m/s², sum to 9 and multiply to 18; the larger is kept as the acceleration acting on a load whose mass is 117 kg. A separate voltmeter reads 13 V, unrelated to this task. The resulting force is scaled by a factor of 6, converted into kilonewtons, and finally scaled once more by a factor of 6. What is the final force, in kilonewtons?

On a lab test bench, two speeds, in m/s, sum to 11 and multiply to 30; the smaller is kept, then tripled. This total speed belongs to a slider whose mass is stated as 41000 grams. The slider's kinetic energy is scaled by a factor of 10, and finally converted into kilojoules. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

On a hydraulic press, the rate at which the ram's acceleration changes follows j(t) = 4t² + 8t (in m/s³, t in seconds) from the start of the stroke; between t = 0 s and t = 3 s, the net change in acceleration has 15 m/s² subtracted from it. This net acceleration acts on a ram whose mass is stated as 136000 grams. From the resulting force, 1 N is subtracted, the total is scaled by a factor of 8, and finally 24 N is subtracted. What is the final force, in newtons?

A machine's final force reading, in kilonewtons after a last addition of 9 kN, is wanted — but it starts with a jerk profile. The rate at which a part's acceleration changes follows j(t) = 4t² + t (in m/s³, t in seconds); between t = 2 s and t = 3 s, the net change in acceleration acts on a part whose mass is stated as 50000 grams. From the resulting force, 18 N is subtracted, the total is converted into kilonewtons, and finally 9 kN is added. What is the final force, in kilonewtons?

On a lab test bench, two speeds of 2 m/s and 19 m/s are added and the sum doubled, giving the effective speed of a slider whose mass is stated as 3000 grams. From the slider's kinetic energy, 21 J is added, then 2 J is subtracted, then 16 J is subtracted again, and finally the total is converted into kilojoules. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

A crane's final force reading, in kilonewtons after a final fivefold scaling, is wanted — but it starts with two acceleration readings. Two readings, in m/s², sum to 15 and multiply to 56; the larger is kept as the acceleration acting on a load whose mass is 113 kg. A separate thermometer reads 33°C, unrelated to this task. The resulting force is converted into kilonewtons, scaled by a factor of 12, and finally scaled once more by a factor of 5. What is the final force, in kilonewtons?

On a machine test rig, the rate at which a part's acceleration changes follows j(t) = 2t² + 7t (in m/s³, t in seconds); between t = 1 s and t = 2 s, the net change in acceleration acts on a part whose mass is stated as 101000 grams. To the resulting force, 3 N is added, then 18 N is subtracted, the total is scaled by a factor of 12, and finally 5 N is added. What is the final force, in newtons?

Two acceleration readings of 3 m/s² and 7 m/s² are added and the sum multiplied by 5, giving the effective acceleration on a machine part whose mass is stated as 80000 grams. The resulting force is scaled by a factor of 5, scaled again by 9, converted into kilonewtons, and finally reduced by 13 kN. What is the final force, in kilonewtons?

Two rods measure 323 cm and 329 cm; the greatest length dividing both evenly is used as the speed, in meters per second, of a slider whose mass is stated as 51000 grams. From the slider's kinetic energy, 9 J is subtracted, the total is scaled by a factor of 9, then 2 J is subtracted again, and finally the result is scaled once more by a factor of 3. What is the final energy, in joules?

On a lab test bench, two speeds of 5 m/s and 10 m/s are added and the sum doubled; to this figure, 4 m/s is added. This total speed belongs to a 60 kg slider. From the slider's kinetic energy, 29 J is subtracted, the total is converted into kilojoules, and finally scaled by a factor of 7. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

A crane's final force reading, in kilonewtons after a final ninefold scaling, is wanted — but it starts with a speed trace. On the crane hook, speed follows v(t) = 4t³ − 5t² (in m/s, t in seconds); its instantaneous acceleration at t = 2.0 s is recorded. This acceleration acts on a load whose mass is stated as 81000 grams. The resulting force is converted into kilonewtons, then increased by 14 kN, increased again by 14 kN, and finally scaled by a factor of 9. What is the final force, in kilonewtons?

On a machine test rig, the rate at which a part's acceleration changes follows j(t) = t² + 8t (in m/s³, t in seconds); between t = 2 s and t = 3 s, the net change in acceleration acts on a part whose mass is stated as 46000 grams. To the resulting force, 4 N is added, the total is scaled by a factor of 8, and finally scaled again by a factor of 5. What is the final force, in newtons?

Two rods measure 144 cm and 54 cm; the greatest length dividing both evenly is used as the speed, in meters per second, of a slider whose mass is stated as 45000 grams. The slider's kinetic energy is doubled, scaled again by a factor of 5, and finally scaled once more by a factor of 5. What is the final energy, in joules?

On a lab test bench, two speeds of 6 m/s and 6 m/s are added and the sum multiplied by 6; to this figure, 2 m/s is added, then 10 m/s is subtracted. This net speed belongs to an 11 kg slider. The slider's kinetic energy is converted into kilojoules, and finally doubled. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

A lab's final energy reading, in kilojoules after a final doubling, is wanted — but it starts with a position trace. On a test bench, a slider's position follows x(t) = 4t³ + 2t² (in meters, t in seconds); its instantaneous speed at t = 2.0 s is recorded, in meters per second. This speed belongs to a slider whose mass is 31 kg. The slider's kinetic energy is converted into kilojoules, then reduced by 12 kJ, then increased by 26 kJ, and finally doubled. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

A lab's final energy reading, in kilojoules after a final sixfold scaling, is wanted — but it starts with two rod lengths. Two rods measure 302 cm and 41 cm; the greatest length dividing both evenly is used as the speed, in meters per second, of a slider whose mass is stated as 49000 grams. The slider's kinetic energy is converted into kilojoules, then reduced by 18 kJ, then increased by 13 kJ, and finally scaled by a factor of 6. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

A machine's final force reading, in newtons after a last addition of 11 N, is wanted — but it starts with a jerk profile. The rate at which a part's acceleration changes follows j(t) = 4t² + 7t (in m/s³, t in seconds) from the start of the test; between t = 0 s and t = 2 s, the net change in acceleration acts on a part whose mass is 126 kg. From the resulting force, 15 N is subtracted, then 25 N is added back, and finally 11 N is added once more. What is the final force, in newtons?

Two rods measure 332 cm and 317 cm; the greatest length dividing both evenly is used as the acceleration, in m/s², of a machine part whose mass is stated as 189000 grams. A separate voltmeter reads 8 V, unrelated to this task. The resulting force is converted into kilonewtons, then scaled by a factor of 9, scaled again by 4, and finally scaled once more by 4. What is the final force, in kilonewtons?

A machine's final force reading, in newtons after two successive additions, is wanted — but it starts with two acceleration readings. Two readings, in m/s², sum to 13 and multiply to 42; the smaller is kept, then multiplied by 10. This total acceleration acts on a 3 kg part, producing a force that is doubled. Finally, 25 N is added, then 21 N is added again. What is the final force, in newtons?

A lab's final energy reading, in kilojoules after a final subtraction of 17 kJ, is wanted — but it starts with a sensor signal. A calibration probe outputs a signal s(t) = 4t³ − t² over time t in seconds; the second rate of change of this signal at t = 2.0 s is read directly as a speed, in meters per second. This speed belongs to a slider whose mass is 23 kg. The slider's kinetic energy is converted into kilojoules, scaled by a factor of 6, scaled again by 4, and finally reduced by 17 kJ. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

A part's position on a test rig follows x(t) = 3t³ − 4t² (in meters, t in seconds); its instantaneous acceleration at t = 2.0 s is recorded. This acceleration acts on a part whose mass is stated as 38000 grams. A separate voltmeter reads 9 V, unrelated to this task. To the resulting force, 2 N is added, the total is converted into kilonewtons, then reduced by 23 kN, and finally scaled by a factor of 8. What is the final force, in kilonewtons?

A lab's final energy reading, in kilojoules after a final subtraction of 1 kJ, is wanted — but it starts with two speed candidates. Two speeds, in m/s, sum to 3 and multiply to 2; the larger is kept, then doubled. This total speed belongs to a 59 kg slider. A separate thermometer reads 26°C, unrelated to this task. The slider's kinetic energy is converted into kilojoules, and finally 1 kJ is subtracted. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

On a crane test rig, two acceleration readings, in m/s², sum to 7 and multiply to 10; the smaller is kept as the acceleration acting on a load whose mass is 88 kg. The resulting force is converted into kilonewtons, scaled by a factor of 6, then reduced by 11 kN, and finally scaled once more by a factor of 11. What is the final force, in kilonewtons?

A machine's final force reading, in kilonewtons, is the goal — reached only after a chain of acceleration adjustments. On a test rig, the rate at which a part's acceleration changes follows j(t) = 4t² + t (in m/s³, t in seconds) from the start of the test; between t = 0 s and t = 3 s, the net change in acceleration has 24 subtracted from it, then 14 added back. This net acceleration acts on a part whose mass is 77 kg. A separate stopwatch reads 60 seconds, unrelated to this task. From the resulting force, 15 N is subtracted, and finally the total is converted into kilonewtons. What is the final force, in kilonewtons?
